what_it_does: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are a style of AI model inspired by biological neurons: instead of sending continuous numerical values between layers, neurons fire a '1' (a spike) or stay silent with a '0.' This extreme simplicity means most values are zero, so hardware can skip enormous amounts of multiplication — saving power. Existing SNN chips exploit this 'most values are zero' property but treat each individual non-zero spike as a separate event to process. Phi observes that these spikes form recurring spatial patterns — groups of neurons tend to fire together in predictable combinations. The system clusters these patterns offline (like sorting a deck of cards into suits), pre-computes the result of each pattern multiplied against the model's weights, and then at runtime simply looks up the pre-computed result rather than doing the math fresh. A thin 'correction' layer handles the small fraction of spikes that don't match any pattern. A purpose-built chip handles both layers simultaneously, achieving further energy savings on top of the basic zero-skipping that SNNs already provide.
